ME404: Dynamics and Control of Mechanical Systems, Fall 2026

Problem Set #4: Midterm Study Guide (Chapters 1–4) — Answer Key

This key follows the notation and diagrams in Problem Set 4. Throughout, Dc​(s) is the controller, G(s) the plant, T(s)=Y/R the closed-loop transfer function, and E=R−Y the system error. Transfer functions use zero initial conditions. Rise time is the interval between the first crossings of 10% and 90% of the final output, overshoot is measured relative to the final output, and settling time uses a 1% band. Every Final Value Theorem (FVT) calculation below is preceded by a stability check, because the theorem is meaningless without one.

The symbolic identities for Problems 2–10 quoted below were rederived, and the sampled response metrics were measured using an independent Runge–Kutta integration in ps4-answers-check.py; Problem 1 and the explanatory prose are not machine-checked. The MATLAB equivalent of the (MATLAB) parts is ps4_answers.m, which was run in MATLAB R2026a and reproduces the same numbers.

Problem #1: Short Answers

(a) What feedback buys and costs

Feedback buys (any two): stabilization of an unstable plant, since open loop cannot move a pole; rejection of disturbances, by the factor S=1/(1+GDc​); insensitivity of the overall gain to plant variation, by the same factor; and tracking without an exact plant model. It costs (any two): a sensor, whose noise reaches the output through T and whose calibration limits the achievable accuracy; control effort, because large loop gain means large u and possible saturation; the possibility of instability, since a stable plant can be destabilized by too much gain; and added complexity. See Feedback Properties, §7.3.

(b) Moving a pole pair radially outward

For a zero-free second-order system, whose response is determined entirely by the pole pair, moving −1±2j to −2±4j keeps the angle from the negative real axis fixed, so ζ=1/5​ is unchanged, while ωn​ doubles from 5​ to 25​ and σ doubles from 1 to 2. Therefore the overshoot, which depends on ζ alone, is unchanged; the rise time tr​≃1.8/ωn​ halves; and the settling time ts​≃4.6/σ halves. The response has the same shape played twice as fast. (If other poles or zeros are present, moving one pair alone does not simply rescale time; that is the lesson of Problem 3.)

(c) Why a right-half-plane zero produces undershoot

Write H(s)=(1−zs​)H0​(s)=H0​(s)−z1​sH0​(s), so that in the time domain y(t)=y0​(t)−z1​y˙​0​(t), where y0​ is the step response of the zero-free second-order part H0​, which has positive DC gain. At t=0+ both y0​ and y˙​0​ are zero, but y˙​0​ grows first: for H0​=ωn2​/(s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​), y0​≈21​ωn2​t2 and y˙​0​≈ωn2​t for small t, so y≈−zωn2​​t. The response leaves zero with a negative slope and goes negative, because the derivative term is of lower order in t and dominates at first; for H4​ of Problem 3, y4​≈−425​t. Later y0​ grows toward its positive final value and the response turns around. With a left-half-plane zero the derivative term enters with a positive sign and, for the underdamped pair used in Problem 3, the same mechanism speeds up the rise and adds overshoot (an overdamped H0​ with a distant LHP zero can stay monotone). (The argument is for this canonical form; a general transfer function with an RHP zero need not start in the wrong direction.)

(d) The Final Value Theorem and Y(s)=3/[s(s2+9)]

The FVT applies only if every pole of sY(s) lies strictly in the left half-plane. Here sY(s)=3/(s2+9) has poles at ±3j, on the imaginary axis, so the hypothesis fails. The formal limit 1/3 is the time average of y(t), not its limit: inverting, y(t)=31​(1−cos3t), which oscillates between 0 and 2/3 forever and has no final value.

(e) Type is robust; error constants are not

For a Type 1 unity-feedback loop, Dc​G contains one integrator, so the position constant Kp​=lims→0​Dc​G is infinite and the step error 1/(1+Kp​) is zero. A 20% gain change does not remove the integrator (and by assumption does not destabilize the loop), so the step error stays zero: type is a structural property. The ramp error is 1/Kv​ with Kv​=lims→0​sDc​G proportional to the loop gain, so it changes inversely with the gain: a 20% gain increase gives Kv′​=1.2Kv​ and a ramp error 1/(1.2Kv​), about 17% smaller, while a 20% decrease raises the error by 25%. The error constant depends on the numbers, not just the structure. See System Type, §5.3.

(f) Which integrator counts for a plant-input disturbance

With W at the plant input and R=0, E/W=−G/(1+Dc​G). A constant disturbance is rejected only if Dc​(0)=∞, that is, only if the controller contains the integrator: in steady state the integrator’s input e must be zero or its output would keep changing, and its constant output supplies the u=−w that cancels the disturbance. An integrator in the plant sits downstream of the disturbance entry point; it integrates u+w, and canceling w then requires a nonzero constant u, which a controller without an integrator can only produce from a nonzero constant error. Only integrators between the error and the point where the disturbance enters count. (This assumes the usual case in which the plant has a nonzero DC response apart from its integrator; a plant with a zero at the origin would block a constant disturbance on its own.)

(g) S+T=1

S(s)+T(s)=1 at every s, including every s=jω. The reference reaches the error through S, an output disturbance reaches the output through S, and sensor noise reaches the output through T. Making ∣S∣ and ∣T∣ both small at the same frequency is impossible, since the identity is between complex numbers and gives ∣S∣+∣T∣≥1. The usual resolution is to make ∣S∣ small at low frequency, where disturbances live, and ∣T∣ small at high frequency, where noise lives. (A disturbance at the plant input reaches the output through GS; the identity then constrains its effect relative to open loop, which is S, rather than the absolute gain ∣GS∣.)

(h) Why Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain tuning fails for G=1/[(s+1)(s+2)]

Under proportional control the characteristic polynomial is s2+3s+2+K, which has all coefficients positive for every K>0: a second-order polynomial with positive coefficients is stable, so no gain produces a sustained (marginal) oscillation; for K>1/4 the response is underdamped, but every oscillation decays. There is no ultimate gain Ku​ and no ultimate period Pu​ to feed into the table. The method needs a plant whose phase reaches −180∘ at a finite frequency, so that a complex pole pair crosses the imaginary axis at finite gain. For a plant without zeros, that means at least third order; a time delay or a right-half-plane zero can supply the extra phase lag at lower order.

(i) Derivative action: not alone for tracking, and filtered in practice

Pure derivative control has zero gain at s=0, so it produces no control action at all in response to a constant error; it can only reshape the transient, never set the steady state, so for setpoint tracking it is paired with P or PI. It is filtered because the gain of kD​s grows without bound with frequency, so high-frequency sensor noise would reach the actuator amplified; the filtered form kD​s/(Tf​s+1) caps the high-frequency gain at kD​/Tf​.

(j) Steady-state response of G=2/(s+2) to 4cos2t

G(j2)=2+2j2​=1+j1​=2​1​∠−45∘, so

yss​(t)=2​4​cos(2t−4π​)=2.83cos(2t−0.785).​

The word steady-state is needed because the complete response also contains a transient Ce−2t from the pole at −2 (needed to satisfy the initial condition); the sinusoid above is what remains after that term has decayed.

Problem #2: Magnetic Levitation, From Physics to a Transfer Function

The model is mx¨=mg−ki2/x2 with m=0.1 kg, k=10−4 Nm2/A2, g=10 m/s2, and x0​=0.05 m. Write it as x¨=f(x,i) with

f(x,i)=g−mk​x2i2​.

(a) Equilibrium current

At equilibrium x¨=0, so the magnetic force balances the weight:

x02​ki02​​=mg⟹i0​=x0​kmg​​=0.0510−4(0.1)(10)​​=0.05×100⟹i0​=5 A.​

(b) Linearization

With x=x0​+δx and i=i0​+δi, expand f to first order about (x0​,i0​), where f(x0​,i0​)=0:

δx¨=∂x∂f​​0​δx+∂i∂f​​0​δi.

The partial derivatives are

∂x∂f​=m2k​x3i2​,∂i∂f​=−m2k​x2i​.

Using the equilibrium relation ki02​/x02​=mg, we simplify these to ∂f/∂x∣0​=2g/x0​ and ∂f/∂i∣0​=−2g/i0​. Numerically,

∂x∂f​​0​=0.052(10)​=400 s−2,∂i∂f​​0​=−52(10)​=−4 m/(s2A),

so

δx¨=400δx−4δi.​

What was thrown away: all terms of second and higher order in δx and δi (for example, δx2, δxδi). The linear model is trustworthy while ∣δx∣≪x0​ and ∣δi∣≪i0​, that is, for gaps within a few millimeters of 5 cm and currents within a fraction of an ampere of 5 A.

The signs are physical: increasing the gap weakens the magnet (1/x2) so the ball accelerates away, a destabilizing spring; increasing the current pulls the ball up, so δi enters with a negative sign on δx¨.

(c) Transfer function, poles, and stability

Taking the Laplace transform with zero initial conditions gives s2δX=400δX−4δI, so

δI(s)δX(s)​=s2−400−4​=(s−20)(s+20)−4​,poles at s=±20 rad/s.​

The pole at +20 makes the open-loop plant unstable. The negative gain says that more current moves the ball up (decreasing x). Physically, the plant is an inverted “spring.” With the current held at i0​, the linear model’s free response is δx(t)=δx0​cosh20t+20δx˙0​​sinh20t, so for a ball displaced δx0​=1 mm and released from rest, δx(t)=δx0​cosh20t. The first doubling, cosh20t=2, takes

t2​=20cosh−12​=201.317​=0.066 s,

and once the decaying e−20t term is negligible, the response grows like 21​δx0​e20t, so the doubling interval approaches ln2/20=0.035 s. (Exactly, the n-th interval is [cosh−12n+1−cosh−12n]/20: 65.8, 37.3, 35.3, 34.8 ms, and so on.) Extrapolating the linear model, a 1 mm displacement reaches 1 cm (a 20% change in the gap, beyond where the linearization is accurate) in about 0.15 s, which is why the ball cannot be held by hand-tuning a constant current.

(d) Positive gain form and the failure of proportional control

With u=−δi,

UδX​=s2−4004​=s2−a2K0​​,K0​=4,a=20.​

Proportional feedback u=−KP​δx (equivalently δi=KP​δx) gives

δx¨=400δx−4KP​δx⟹s2+(4KP​−400)=0.

There is no s1 term, so Routh’s necessary condition fails for every KP​ and the loop is never asymptotically stable. For KP​<100 the roots are real, ±400−4KP​​, and one is in the right half-plane. At KP​=100 there is a double pole at the origin and δx(t)=A+Bt drifts. For KP​>100 the roots are ±j4KP​−400​, on the imaginary axis: the ball oscillates about the set point without decaying, at a frequency that grows with KP​. Proportional control turns an unstable “negative spring” into a positive spring but adds no damping. The controller must add a term proportional to δx˙ (derivative or rate feedback), or a lead compensator as in Problem Set 3.

(e) PD control

With δi=KP​δx+KD​δx˙,

δx¨=400δx−4KP​δx−4KD​δx˙⟹s2+4KD​s+(4KP​−400)=0.​

A second-order polynomial is stable if and only if all coefficients are positive:

KD​>0,KP​>100 A/m.​

The target polynomial is (s+20)2+202=s2+40s+800. Matching coefficients,

4KD​=40 ⇒ KD​=10 As/m​,4KP​−400=800 ⇒ KP​=300 A/m.​

The closed loop then has ωn​=800​=28.3 rad/s and ζ=0.707.

All six transfer functions have unit DC gain, so every step response ends at y∞​=1 and overshoot is measured relative to 1.

(b) Matching to the panels

Measured values (from the check script; MATLAB’s stepinfo with the stated options reproduces them to the digits shown):

(i) Mp​≤10%: H1​,H3​,H6​. (ii) tr​≤0.4 s: H1​,H2​,H4​,H5​. (iii) ts​≤1.5 s: H1​,H3​,H6​. Only H1​ meets all three.​ Note that H6​ fails the rise-time specification by exactly the first-order formula, tr​=ln9/5=0.439 s, even though its settling time is the best of the six.

Two cautions about deciding (c) by hand. First, 4.6/σ is an envelope estimate: it predicts 1.53 s for H1​, which would fail (iii), while the last entry into the 1% band is actually at 1.25 s. Second, H5​ settles at 1.56 s, too close to the 1.5 s line to read from the figure. Decide the clear cases from the figure and the formulas, flag these two, and let stepinfo in (d) settle them. On the exam the thresholds are chosen far enough from the responses that the figure decides.

(d) (MATLAB) Comparison with the predictions

stepinfo with the stated options reproduces the table in (c), as does the Python check script. The second-order formulas are furthest off for H5​ (predicted 9.5% overshoot and 0.36 s rise, measured 76% and 0.08 s) and for H3​ (predicted 0.36 s rise, measured 0.58 s). In H5​ the zero at −2 is closer to the origin than the poles’ real part, so the derivative term 21​y˙​1​ is comparable to y1​ itself and dominates the early response. In H3​ the extra pole at −4 is only 1.3 times σ, far short of the factor of four or more needed for the dominant-pair approximation, so its slow mode is a large part of the response. Note also that the actual settling time of H1​ (1.25 s) is shorter than the 4.6/σ=1.53 s estimate: the rule is an estimate of the envelope, and the last 1% band crossing happens earlier.

Problem #4: Laplace Solution of Initial-Value Problems and the Final Value Theorem

The derivative rules are L{y˙​}=sY(s)−y(0) and L{y¨​}=s2Y(s)−sy(0)−y˙​(0).

(a) y¨​+3y˙​+2y=4⋅1(t), y(0)=1, y˙​(0)=0

Predict. The homogeneous equation has characteristic polynomial s2+3s+2=(s+1)(s+2): natural poles at −1 and −2, both in the LHP, so the natural response decays. The step forcing adds a pole at s=0 to Y(s), which carries the constant final value.

Solve. Transforming,

s2Y−s(1)−0+3(sY−1)+2Y=s4​⟹(s2+3s+2)Y=s+3+s4​=ss2+3s+4​.

Y(s)=s(s+1)(s+2)s2+3s+4​=sA​+s+1B​+s+2C​.

Cover-up: A=(1)(2)4​=2, B=(−1)(1)1−3+4​=−2, C=(−2)(−1)4−6+4​=1. Hence

y(t)=2−2e−t+e−2t,t≥0.​

Verify. y(0)=2−2+1=1 ✓; y˙​(t)=2e−t−2e−2t so y˙​(0)=0 ✓. Substituting, y¨​=−2e−t+4e−2t, and y¨​+3y˙​+2y=(−2+6−4)e−t+(4−6+2)e−2t+4=4 ✓. FVT: sY(s)=(s+1)(s+2)s2+3s+4​ has poles at −1,−2, strictly in the LHP, so the theorem applies and y(∞)=lims→0​sY=4/2=2, which agrees with y(t)→2. This is the final value, the forcing amplitude 4 times the DC gain 1/2 of 1/(s2+3s+2); the initial conditions only affect the decaying terms.

(b) y¨​+4y=8⋅1(t), y(0)=0, y˙​(0)=2

Predict. Characteristic polynomial s2+4: natural poles at ±2j, on the imaginary axis, so the natural response is a persistent oscillation at 2 rad/s that neither grows nor decays. The forcing adds a pole at s=0.

Solve.

s2Y−s(0)−2+4Y=s8​⟹Y(s)=s2+42+8/s​=s(s2+4)2s+8​=sA​+s2+4Bs+C​.

Cover-up at s=0: A=8/4=2. Matching numerators, 2s+8=2(s2+4)+(Bs+C)s=(2+B)s2+Cs+8, so B=−2 and C=2:

Y(s)=s2​−s2+42s​+s2+42​⟹y(t)=2−2cos2t+sin2t,t≥0.​

Verify. y(0)=2−2=0 ✓; y˙​=4sin2t+2cos2t, y˙​(0)=2 ✓; y¨​=8cos2t−4sin2t, and y¨​+4y=8cos2t−4sin2t+8−8cos2t+4sin2t=8 ✓. FVT: sY(s)=s2+42s+8​ has poles at ±2j, so the hypothesis fails. The formal limit lims→0​sY(s)=8/4=2 exists, but it is not the final value: y(t) oscillates about 2 with amplitude 22+12​=5​ forever. The number 2 is the average of the oscillation, which is all the formula can extract once an undamped mode is present.

(c) y˙​+2y=2r, r=t, y(0)=1

Predict. Characteristic polynomial s+2: one natural pole at −2, decaying. The ramp forcing 2/s2 adds a double pole at the origin.

Solve.

sY−1+2Y=s22​⟹Y(s)=s+21+2/s2​=s2(s+2)s2+2​=sA​+s2B​+s+2C​.

Cover-up on the highest powers: B=0+20+2​=1 (multiply by s2, set s=0) and C=44+2​=23​. The coefficient A of the simple pole inside a repeated pole is not given by cover-up; match the s2 coefficients of s2+2=As(s+2)+B(s+2)+Cs2: 1=A+C, so A=−21​. (Check the s1 coefficient: 0=2A+B=−1+1 ✓.)

y(t)=t−21​+23​e−2t,t≥0.​

Verify. y(0)=−21​+23​=1 ✓. y˙​=1−3e−2t, and y˙​+2y=1−3e−2t+2t−1+3e−2t=2t ✓. FVT: sY(s)=s(s+2)s2+2​ still has a pole at s=0, so the hypothesis fails; the formal limit is lims→0​sY(s)=+∞, and indeed y→∞, as a ramp into a stable system with nonzero DC gain must.

The tracking lag. y(t)−r(t)=−21​+23​e−2t→−21​​: in steady state the output is a ramp with the same unit slope as r (the system has unit DC gain), running a constant 21​ below it. Since t−21​=r(t−21​), the output is the reference delayed by 0.5 s​, one time constant of the system. The lag is the coefficient A=−21​ of the 1/s term in the expansion of the double pole at the origin: the 1/s2 term reproduces the ramp, the 1/s term is the constant offset, and the 1/(s+2) term is the transient. This is exactly the structure of a Type 1 ramp error: the system follows the ramp but not at zero error.

Problem #5: A Two-Loop Block Diagram With a Disturbance and a Feedforward Path

(a) Transfer functions

Label the signal that enters G2​, after the disturbance has been added, V. The signal equations are

E=R−Y,V=G1​E+G3​R+W−H1​Y,Y=G2​V.

Substituting,

Y=G2​[G1​(R−Y)+G3​R+W−H1​Y]⟹Y(1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​)=G2​(G1​+G3​)R+G2​W,

so

RY​=1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​G2​(G1​+G3​)​,WY​=1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​G2​​.​

For the system error, E=R−Y gives

RE​=1−RY​=1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​1+G2​H1​−G2​G3​​,WE​=−WY​=1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​−G2​​.​

Block reduction check for Y/R. Collapse the inner loop first: G2​ with negative feedback H1​ becomes G2​/(1+G2​H1​). Its input is G1​E+G3​R. Then

Y=1+G2​H1​G2​​[G1​(R−Y)+G3​R] ⟹ Y[1+1+G2​H1​G1​G2​​]=1+G2​H1​G2​(G1​+G3​)​R,

and multiplying through by 1+G2​H1​ recovers the same Y/R.

(b) Limiting cases

  • G3​=0: from the diagram, R reaches the inner junction only through the outer loop, so the system is G1​ in series with the inner loop, inside unity feedback. The formula gives Y/R=G1​G2​/(1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​), which is the series connection G1​⋅G2​/(1+G2​H1​) closed with unity feedback ✓. Y/W is unchanged, as it must be, since W never passes through G3​.
  • H1​=0: the inner loop disappears and the forward path is G2​ driven by G1​E+G3​R+W. The formula gives Y/R=G2​(G1​+G3​)/(1+G1​G2​) and Y/W=G2​/(1+G1​G2​) ✓: the feedforward path adds G2​G3​R to the numerator but does not change the loop, so the denominator is just 1+G1​G2​.

(c) Numbers

With G1​=K, G2​=1/[s(s+2)], H1​=kt​s, G3​=0, the denominator 1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​=1+s(s+2)K+kt​s​, so the characteristic polynomial is

s(s+2)+kt​s+K=s2+(2+kt​)s+K.​

Rate feedback adds to the damping coefficient only. For K=25 and kt​=3: s2+5s+25, poles

s=−2.5±j25−6.25​=−2.5±4.33j​,ωn​=5,ζ=2⋅55​=0.5.

Y/R=25/(s2+5s+25) has no zero, so the overshoot formula is exact:

Mp​=e−0.5π/0.75​=e−1.814=16.3%​.

Without the tachometer (kt​=0) the same K would give s2+2s+25, ζ=0.2, and Mp​=53%: the rate feedback raises the damping ratio from 0.2 to 0.5 at no cost in ωn​.

The loop is stable (positive coefficients, second order), so the FVT applies to E/W=−1/(s2+5s+25) with W=1/s:

ess​=s→0lim​s⋅s2+5s+25−1​⋅s1​=−251​​.

The output settles at +1/25 per unit of constant disturbance; the loop is Type 0 with respect to W because the only integrator is in G2​, downstream of the disturbance entry.

(d) Exact tracking by feedforward

Setting Y/R=1 in (a):

G2​(G1​+G3​)=1+G1​G2​+G2​H1​⟹G2​G3​=1+G2​H1​⟹G3​=G2​1​+H1​=s(s+2)+kt​s.

With the numbers, G3​=s2+5s​, the plant inverse plus the rate-feedback term. It is improper: it asks for the first and second derivatives of the reference, so it has unbounded gain at high frequency and cannot be realized exactly (a realizable version adds fast poles and is then only approximately an inverse). If it could be built, any noise on r would be differentiated twice and would reach the plant input amplified. This is plant inversion, the feedforward idea of PID Tuning, §8: it works for the smooth, low-frequency part of the reference and must be paired with feedback for everything else.

Problem #6: DC Motor Position Control With Rate Feedback and Integral Action

The parameters are a1​=50 s−1, b0​=100 rad/(Vs2), c0​=5 rad/(Nms2).

(a) Block diagram and closed-loop transfer functions

Taking the Laplace transform of the motor equation gives (s2+a1​s)Θm​=b0​Va​+c0​W, and transforming the control law gives Va​=K(Θr​−Θm​−TD​sΘm​). Substituting,

(s2+a1​s)Θm​=b0​KΘr​−b0​KΘm​−b0​KTD​sΘm​+c0​W

Θr​Θm​​=s2+(a1​+b0​KTD​)s+b0​Kb0​K​,WΘm​​=s2+(a1​+b0​KTD​)s+b0​Kc0​​.​

Neither has a zero: the rate term sits in the feedback path, so it changes only the damping coefficient of the denominator. (Had the derivative acted on the error, K(1+TD​s)e, the numerator would contain the zero −1/TD​.)

(b) Open-loop steady speed

With w=0 and constant va​=100 V, the speed equation ω˙+a1​ω=b0​va​ settles at

ωss​=a1​b0​va​​=50100×100​=200 rad/s=200×2π60​=1910 rpm.​

(c) Design region and gains

Overshoot at most 5%: e−ζπ/1−ζ2​≤0.05 gives ζπ/1−ζ2​≥ln20=2.996, so

ζ≥π2+ln220​ln20​=4.3412.996​=0.690.

Settling time at most 0.1 s with the envelope estimate ts​≃4.6/σ: σ≥46 s−1. Because the estimate is approximate, so is the region: a pair at exactly −46±46j actually settles in 0.101 s. That is why the chosen poles should sit inside the region with margin and the design should be checked. The region is the intersection of the half-plane Res≤−46 with the wedge ∣∠∣≤cos−10.690=46.4∘ measured from the negative real axis. (Sketch: a vertical line at −46 and two rays from the origin at ±46.4∘ from the negative real axis; the admissible region is to the left of the line and inside the wedge.)

Poles at −50±50j have σ=50>46 and ζ=cos45∘=0.707>0.690: inside the region with margin on both constraints. The predicted overshoot is e−π=4.3% and the predicted settling time 4.6/50=0.092 s (measured in (g): 0.093 s, within the specification). The target polynomial is (s+50)2+502=s2+100s+5000. Matching with the denominator in (a):

b0​K=5000 ⇒ K=50 V/rad​,a1​+b0​KTD​=100 ⇒ 50+5000TD​=100 ⇒ TD​=0.01 s​.

Because Θm​/Θr​ has no zero and is exactly second order, the overshoot formula is exact for this design; only the settling-time estimate is approximate.

(d) Error to the reference

Θr​E​=1−Θr​Θm​​=s2+100s+5000s2+100s​=s2+100s+5000s(s+100)​.

One zero at the origin, so the loop is Type 1 with respect to the reference. The loop is stable (positive coefficients), so the FVT applies: for a step of 1 rad, ess​=lims→0​E/Θr​=0; for a unit ramp, ess​=lims→0​s1​Θr​E​=5000100​=501​, so

Kv​=a1​+b0​KTD​b0​K​=1005000​=50 s−1,ess,step​=0,ess,ramp​=0.02 rad.​

With proportional control alone at the same K (TD​=0), Kv​=b0​K/a1​=100. The rate feedback halves Kv​: it buys damping (ζ rises from 0.354 to 0.707) at the price of doubling the ramp error. This is the tachometer tradeoff of System Type, §6.3.

(e) Error to a load torque

With θr​=0, E=−Θm​, so

WE​=s2+100s+5000−c0​​.

There is no zero at the origin: Type 0 with respect to the disturbance. For w=1 Nm,

ess​=s→0lim​s2+100s+5000−c0​​=−50005​=−0.001 rad​,

that is, the shaft settles 1 mrad past the reference in the direction the torque pushes it. The integrator in the motor does not help because it lies downstream of the torque.

(f) Integral action

With Va​=K(E−TD​sΘm​)+skI​​E and E=Θr​−Θm​,

(s2+a1​s)Θm​=b0​[K+skI​​](Θr​−Θm​)−b0​KTD​sΘm​+c0​W.

Multiply by s and collect Θm​:

Θm​[s3+(a1​+b0​KTD​)s2+b0​Ks+b0​kI​]=b0​(Ks+kI​)Θr​+c0​sW.

a(s)=s3+100s2+5000s+100kI​,WE​=s3+100s2+5000s+100kI​−c0​s​.​

E/W now has a zero at the origin, so the loop is Type 1 with respect to the disturbance: a constant torque produces zero steady-state error. Routh array:

s3s2s1s0​1100100100⋅5000−100kI​​=5000−kI​100kI​​5000100kI​​

For all first-column entries to be positive, we need 0<kI​<5000​. For a unit-ramp torque, W=1/s2, with the loop stable,

ess​=s→0lim​s⋅a(s)−c0​s​⋅s21​=100kI​−c0​​=−20kI​1​ rad​.

At one-tenth of the limit, kI​=500, this is −10−4 rad​ per Nm/s of ramp rate. The closed-loop poles for kI​=500 (from the check script) are −12.9 and −43.6±44.5j: the complex pair has moved in slightly from −50±50j, and a slow real pole near −13, now the dominant pole, has appeared, which is the usual price of integral action.

Measured: Mp​=4.32% (exactly e−π) and ts​=0.093 s, both inside the specifications and matching (c).

Without integral action, the angle settles at c0​/(b0​K)=0.001 rad, as predicted in (e); with kI​=500, it returns to zero, as predicted in (f), with the slow pole at −12.9 visible in the long tail. Closed-loop poles with integral action: −12.90, −43.55±44.50j. See ps4_answers.m.

As a single fraction,

Dc​(s)=kP​TI​sTI​TD​s2+TI​s+1​.

P (Dc​=10): Dc​G=s(s+1)(s+4)10​ has one integrator, so the loop is Type 1:

Kv​=s→0lim​sDc​G=410​=2.5 s−1,ess,ramp​=Kv​1​=0.4​.

designclosed-loop polesovershoot1% settling
P−4.60, −0.20±1.46j62%22 s

The PI design is the barely stable one: its dominant pair −0.029±1.34j has ζ=0.02, so the response rings for minutes and overshoots by 100%. The integrator’s phase lag has pushed the plant, which was already only a factor of two below its stability limit under P control, almost onto the imaginary axis. Ziegler–Nichols rules were fitted to process plants with delay for a quarter-decay ratio, which is itself about 50% overshoot; they give a starting point in the right order of magnitude, with no guarantee of stability or of acceptable damping, after which the gains (here, kP​ halved and TI​ lengthened) must be adjusted to the actual plant and specifications. Problem #8: System Type With Respect to the Reference and the Disturbance

(Part A) G=1/[(s+1)(s+2)], Dc​=K(s+a)/(s+b)

(i) Dc​G=(s+b)(s+1)(s+2)K(s+a)​. The plant has no integrator, so Type 1 requires the controller pole to sit at the origin: b=0​ (with Ka=0, so that the integrator is not canceled), a PI controller K(s+a)/s=K+Ka/s. Then

Kv​=s→0lim​ss(s+1)(s+2)K(s+a)​=2Ka​​.

(ii) With b=0,

s(s+1)(s+2)+K(s+a)=s3+3s2+(2+K)s+Ka.​

s3s2s1s0​1333(2+K)−Ka​Ka​2+KKa​

With K>0 and a>0, as the problem assumes, the s0 entry is positive, and the s1 entry requires 3(2+K)>Ka:

a<3+K6​(with K>0, a>0).​

(iii) The bound 3+6/K decreases toward 3 as K→∞, so the loop is stable for every positive K if and only if 0<a≤3​. (At a=3 the s1 entry is [3(2+K)−3K]/3=2>0 for every K.) In root-locus terms: with three poles and one zero, the two asymptotes are vertical lines through the centroid [(0−1−2)−(−a)]/2=(a−3)/2, which must not lie in the right half-plane, so a≤3.

(iv) a=1, K=4, b=0: s3+3s2+6s+4. Routh s1 entry: (18−4)/3=14/3>0, stable ✓. Try s=−1: −1+3−6+4=0, so

s3+3s2+6s+4=(s+1)(s2+2s+4)​,poles −1, −1±j3​.

The controller zero at −1 cancels the closed-loop pole at −1 in T=(s+1)(s2+2s+4)4(s+1)​=s2+2s+44​, so the reference step response shows only the complex pair. The mode at −1 is still a closed-loop mode: it appears in the response to a plant-input disturbance, where nothing cancels it.

Kv​=Ka/2=2, so ess,step​=0,ess,ramp​=21​.​

(Part B) G=1/s2, Dc​=8(s+1)/(s+4)

(i) 1+Dc​G=0 gives s2(s+4)+8(s+1)=s3+4s2+8s+8​.

s3s2s1s0​14432−8​=68​88​

No sign changes: stable ✓. Since s=−2 is a root (−8+16−16+8=0),

(s+2)(s2+2s+4),poles −2, −1±j3​.​

(ii) Dc​G=s2(s+4)8(s+1)​ has two integrators: Type 2, with

Ka​=s→0lim​s2Dc​G=48​=2​,ess​: step 0,ramp 0,parabola Ka​1​=21​​.

(iii) With R=0 and the torque at the plant input, Y=G(U+W) and U=−Dc​Y, so Y(1+Dc​G)=GW:

WY​=1+Dc​GG​=1+s2(s+4)8(s+1)​1/s2​=s3+4s2+8s+8s+4​,WE​=−WY​=s3+4s2+8s+8−(s+4)​.​

No zero at the origin: Type 0 with respect to the disturbance, with To,w​(0)=−4/8=−21​, so K0,w​=−2 in the signed convention of the notes and, for a unit-step torque,

ess​=−21​​,

that is, the attitude settles at +0.5 rad per unit of constant torque.

(iv) Both integrators are in the plant, downstream of the point where the torque enters. Rejecting a constant torque requires a constant u=−w from the controller, and a controller without an integrator can only produce that from a nonzero constant error. For the reference, both plant integrators lie between the error and the output, so both count and the loop is Type 2. For the disturbance, only integrators between the error and the disturbance entry (those in Dc​) count, and there are none.

(v) With the disturbance added to the attitude itself, Y=GU+W and U=−Dc​Y, so Y(1+Dc​G)=W:

WY​=1+Dc​G1​=s3+4s2+8s+8s2(s+4)​,WE​=s3+4s2+8s+8−s2(s+4)​.​

Two zeros at the origin: Type 2 with respect to an output disturbance, so a constant offset (and even a ramping one) produces zero steady-state error, and ess​=−21​ to a parabola. The type changed because the disturbance now enters after the plant: both plant integrators lie between the error and the disturbance entry, so both now count. E/W for an output disturbance is just −S(s), the same sensitivity function that governs the reference error, which is why the type with respect to an output disturbance always equals the type with respect to the reference. (Had W instead been an offset in the sensor, the loop would drive the measured attitude X+W to zero and the physical attitude would settle at X=−W: feedback regulates what it measures.)

Problem #9: Robustness of System Type and Sensitivity

Let P(s)=K0​/(2s+1).

(a) Choosing the gains

System (a). L=sK1​​2s+1K0​​, so

RE​=1+L1​=s(2s+1)+K0​K1​s(2s+1)​=2s2+s+K0​K1​s(2s+1)​.

The characteristic polynomial 2s2+s+K0​K1​ is second order with positive coefficients for K0​K1​>0: stable. Step: ess​=lims→0​E/R=0 for any K1​. Ramp: ess​=lims→0​s1​RE​=K0​K1​1​=21​ with K0​=1 gives K1​=2​.

System (b). Y=1+K3​PK3​P​K2​R, so

RY​=2s+1+K3​K0​K2​K3​K0​​,RE​=1−RY​=2s+1+K3​K0​2s+1+K3​K0​−K2​K3​K0​​.

The single pole is at −(1+K3​K0​)/2<0: stable. Step: ess​=1+K3​K0​1+K3​K0​−K2​K3​K0​​=0 requires

K2​=K3​K0​1+K3​K0​​.

With that choice the numerator of E/R collapses to 2s, so E/R=2s+1+K3​K0​2s​ and the ramp error is 1+K3​K0​2​=21​, giving K3​K0​=3. With K0​=1:

K3​=3,K2​=34​.​

(b) Plant gain K0​=1+δ

System (a). E/R=2s2+s+2(1+δ)s(2s+1)​, still stable for δ>−1. The zero at the origin survives, so

ess,step​=0,ess,ramp​=2(1+δ)1​=115​=0.455 at δ=0.1.

System (b). With K2​=4/3 and K3​=3 fixed,

RE​=2s+1+3(1+δ)2s+1+3(1+δ)−4(1+δ)​=2s+4+3δ2s−δ​,

so

ess,step​=4+3δ−δ​=−431​=−0.023 at δ=0.1,eramp​(t)=−4+3δδ​t+(4+3δ)28(1+δ)​+(a term decaying as e−(4+3δ)t/2),

valid while the loop is stable, δ>−34​. At δ=0.1 the asymptote is −t/43+0.476, so the ramp error grows without bound: negatively for δ>0 (the output outruns the ramp) and positively for −34​<δ<0. At δ=0 the slope vanishes and the constant is the finite 21​ of part (a).

The zero steady-state error of system (b) was obtained by cancellation: the input gain was calibrated to the plant gain, and any mismatch leaves a residual. By the course definition ess​=lims→0​[1−T(s)]/sk, system (b) is Type 1 at the nominal calibration (its loop contains no integrator, but 1−Tb​=2s/(2s+4) has a zero at the origin) and drops to Type 0 for any δ=0: its type is a calibration, not a structural property. System (a) has the robust type​: its zero step error comes from the integrator, which forces the error to zero for any plant gain that keeps the loop stable; only its ramp error (an error constant) moves with δ.

(c) Poles and transient response

System (a). 2s2+s+2=0, that is s2+0.5s+1=0: ωn​=1, ζ=0.25, poles −0.25±0.968j​. No zero, so the overshoot formula is exact:

Mp​=e−0.25π/1−0.0625​=e−0.811=44%,ts​≃0.254.6​=18 s (measured 17.3 s).

System (b). Pole at −(1+3)/2=−2​, first order with τ=0.5 s: no overshoot, ts​=ln100/2=2.3 s.

The price of the robust type is the transient: the integrator adds a pole at the origin to a loop that had only one, producing a lightly damped second-order response that overshoots by 44% and takes eight times longer to settle than system (b). A PI controller, or rate feedback, would recover the damping; this is the tradeoff that the root-locus lectures resolve.

(d) Sensitivities

For system (a), Ta​(0)=1+L(0)L(0)​ with L(0)=∞, so Ta​(0)=1 for every K0​: SK0​T​=1+L(0)1​=0​. For system (b), Tb​(0)=1+K3​K0​K2​K3​K0​​ and

SK0​T​=Tb​K0​​∂K0​∂Tb​​=1+K3​K0​1​=41​​

at the nominal values (a 10% plant-gain change produces about a 2.5% DC-gain change, consistent with the −0.023 step error of (b)). The input gain K2​ sits outside the loop, so Tb​∝K2​ and

SK2​T​=1​.

Feedback protects the forward-path parameters (plant and controller gains) by the factor 1/(1+L), and protects the DC gain against them completely when the loop contains an integrator, as long as the loop stays stable. It gives no protection to a prefilter such as K2​, which sits outside the loop. A sensor gain H is inside the loop but is not protected either: with T=L/(1+LH), SHT​=−LH/(1+LH)→−1 at high loop gain, because the loop faithfully drives the measured output to the reference. Both the prefilter and the sensor must therefore be calibrated to the full required accuracy.

Problem #10: Sinusoids, Harmonics, and a Low-Pass Filter

G(s)=1/(0.1s+1) has one pole at −10 and is stable, so a steady-state response exists. Its frequency response is

G(jω)=1+0.1jω1​,∣G(jω)∣=1+0.01ω2​1​,∠G(jω)=−tan−1(0.1ω).

(a) Two sinusoids

G(j10)=1+j1​=2​1​∠−45∘,G(j30)=1+3j1​=10​1​∠−71.57∘.

Each cosine is multiplied by the magnitude and shifted by the phase at its own frequency:

yss​(t)=2​2​cos(10t−4π​)+10​1​cos(30t+4π​−tan−13)=1.414cos(10t−0.785)+0.316cos(30t−0.464),​

with the phases in radians (−45∘ and −26.57∘), the natural unit when t is in seconds and ω in rad/s.

The two components may be treated separately because the system is linear: the response to a sum is the sum of the responses, and each sinusoid is itself a pair of complex exponentials e±jωt that the system maps to G(±jω)e±jωt. Each component must use G at its own frequency.

(b) Fourier coefficients of the square wave

T=π/5 and ω0​=2π/T=10 rad/s, so ω0​T=2π. With ck​=T1​∫0T​u(t)e−jkω0​tdt,

ck​=T1​[∫0T/2​e−jkω0​tdt−∫T/2T​e−jkω0​tdt]=T1​⋅−jkω0​1​[(e−jkπ−1)−(e−j2kπ−e−jkπ)].

Since e−j2kπ=1 and e−jkπ=(−1)k, the bracket is 2[(−1)k−1], and with ω0​T=2π,

ck​=jkω0​T2[1−(−1)k]​=jkπ1−(−1)k​=⎩⎨⎧​jkπ2​,0,​k odd,k even,​​

and c0​=0 directly (zero mean). Odd symmetry makes the coefficients purely imaginary, as expected. Pairing ±k:

ck​ejkω0​t+c−k​e−jkω0​t=2Re[jkπ2​ejkω0​t]=kπ4​sinkω0​t,

so

u(t)=π4​sin10t+3π4​sin30t+5π4​sin50t+⋯=1.273sin10t+0.424sin30t+0.255sin50t+⋯​

(At the switching instants the series converges to the midpoint 0 rather than to ±1; this affects neither the coefficients nor the filtered output.)

(c) Output harmonics

Each term ck​ejkω0​t of the input is a complex exponential, and a stable LTI system responds to est in steady state with G(s)est (the eigenfunction property). By superposition the output is ∑k​G(jkω0​)ck​ejkω0​t, so dk​=G(jkω0​)ck​​. The real amplitude of the k-th harmonic is kπ4​∣G(j10k)∣:

kinput amplitude 4/(kπ)∣G(j10k)∣output amplitude
11.2731/2​=0.7070.900​
30.4241/10​=0.3160.134​
50.2551/26​=0.1960.050​

At the input the third harmonic is 1/3=0.333 of the fundamental; at the output it is

0.9000.134​=31​⋅∣G(j10)∣∣G(j30)∣​=31​102​​=0.149​.

The filter attenuates the third harmonic by an extra factor of 0.447 relative to the fundamental: that is what low-pass means, and it is why the output (a rounded, nearly triangular wave) is smoother than the square-wave input. Far above 10 rad/s, ∣G∣≈10/ω, so the output coefficients fall like 1/k2 instead of 1/k, the signature of a continuous waveform with slope discontinuities rather than jumps.

(d) The transient

The complete response from rest is the steady-state series plus a term from the pole at −10: y(t)=yss​(t)+Ce−10t with C=−yss​(0) chosen so that y(0)=0. The time constant is τ=0.1 s​; the transient is below 1% of its initial size after 4.6τ=0.46 s, so after about half a second (less than one period, since T=π/5=0.63 s) the harmonic description is accurate. Before that, the output is the steady-state waveform shifted by a decaying exponential.

(e) (MATLAB) Simulation

The transient has decayed within about 0.5 s, after which the simulated output and the three-term (harmonics 1, 3, 5) reconstruction differ only by the truncation of the series: that difference peaks at about 0.10 near the corners of the response, roughly 11% of the output’s peak value tanh(π/2)=0.917, and shrinks as more harmonics are kept. See ps4_answers.m for the lsim version.
